new_entities.name: Tea consumption
aliases: black, green, oolong, or mate tea intake
new_entities.description: Habitual consumption of non-herbal tea beverages.

edges.effect_quant: The broad bladder-cancer literature on tea is mostly close to null, though some newer prospective syntheses suggest a very small downward dose-response signal.
edges.mechanism: Tea polyphenols and catechins could plausibly affect urothelial oxidative stress and carcinogen metabolism, but any true effect appears weak at population level. The lack of a strong consistent epidemiologic signal suggests that beverage subtype, smoking, and other lifestyle confounding matter more than a simple universal tea effect.
edges.summary: The most boring conclusion is the right one here: tea does not show a robust bladder-cancer signal. A dose-response bladder-specific meta-analysis was essentially neutral, while broader prospective syntheses hint at a slight protective association that is too small and inconsistent to justify a stronger claim.
edges.caveats: This edge pools different tea subtypes and populations, which likely dilutes any beverage-specific effect. Smoking remains the dominant bladder-cancer confounder in this literature and makes tiny associations hard to interpret confidently.

evidence.citation: Weng H et al 2016 Front Physiol
evidence.notes: Tea Consumption and Risk of Bladder Cancer: A Dose-Response Meta-Analysis.
